# Thermochemistry — 2.1 Heat and Temperature

::: concept T-temperature
term: Temperature
definition: [p.6: "Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample of matter."]
plain: Temperature measures how much kinetic energy the particles in a sample have on average. [p.6: "Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles"]
misconception: Wrong: temperature and heat are the same thing. | Right: temperature does not depend on the amount of matter, but the amount of heat transferred does. [p.6: "Temperature does not depend on the amount of matter present, whereas the amount of heat transferred does."]
:::

::: concept T-heat
term: Heat
definition: [p.6: "Heat (q) is the transfer of thermal energy between two bodies at different temperatures."]
plain: Heat is thermal energy moving from one body to another because the two are at different temperatures. [p.6: "Heat (q) is the transfer of thermal energy between two bodies at different temperatures."]
why: Heat flows on its own from the hotter body to the colder one until both reach the same temperature. [p.6: "Heat always flows spontaneously from a hotter body to a colder body until both reach the same temperature."]
example: A bathtub of warm water and a cup of water at the same temperature can transfer very different amounts of heat. [p.6: "A bathtub of warm water and a cup of water at the same temperature can transfer very different amounts of heat."]
misconception: Wrong: heat is something an object contains. | Right: heat is the transfer of thermal energy between bodies at different temperatures. [p.6: "Heat (q) is the transfer of thermal energy between two bodies at different temperatures."]
:::

::: concept T-system
term: System
definition: [p.7: "The system is the specific portion of matter being studied, such as the chemicals reacting in a flask."]
plain: To study heat flow, chemists split the universe in two, and the system is the part being studied. [p.7: "To study heat flow, chemists divide the universe into two parts."] [p.7: "The system is the specific portion of matter being studied"]
:::

::: concept T-surroundings
term: Surroundings
definition: [p.7: "The surroundings are everything outside the system that can exchange energy with it."]
plain: The surroundings are the rest of the universe: everything outside the system that can exchange energy with it. [p.7: "The surroundings are everything outside the system that can exchange energy with it."]
:::

::: concept T-endothermic-process
term: Endothermic process
definition: [p.7: "An endothermic process absorbs heat from the surroundings, so the surroundings become colder."]
plain: In an endothermic process heat flows into the system, so the surroundings get colder. [p.7: "In an endothermic process, heat flows into the system from the surroundings."] [p.7: "so the surroundings become colder"]
example: Melting ice is endothermic. [p.7: "Melting ice is endothermic."]
misconception: Wrong: an endothermic process makes the surroundings warmer. | Right: it absorbs heat from the surroundings, so they become colder. [p.7: "An endothermic process absorbs heat from the surroundings, so the surroundings become colder."]
:::

::: concept T-exothermic-process
term: Exothermic process
definition: [p.7: "An exothermic process releases heat to the surroundings, so the surroundings become warmer."]
plain: In an exothermic process heat flows out of the system, so the surroundings get warmer. [p.7: "In an exothermic process, heat flows out of the system."] [p.7: "so the surroundings become warmer"]
example: Burning wood is exothermic. [p.7: "Burning wood is exothermic."]
:::

::: figure FIG-2.1
what: The diagram shows heat flowing into the system in an endothermic process and out of the system in an exothermic process. [p.7: "In an endothermic process, heat flows into the system from the surroundings. In an exothermic process, heat flows out of the system."]
:::

::: question Q-2.1-01
type: mcq
bloom: understand
ask: A reaction in a beaker makes the beaker feel colder. What kind of process is it?
option A: Endothermic, because it absorbs heat from the surroundings.
option B: Exothermic, because it releases heat to the surroundings.
option C: Endothermic, because it releases heat to the surroundings.
option D: Neither, because a temperature change has nothing to do with heat.
answer: A
why: An endothermic process absorbs heat from the surroundings, so the surroundings become colder. [p.7: "An endothermic process absorbs heat from the surroundings, so the surroundings become colder."]
why-not B: An exothermic process makes the surroundings warmer, not colder. [p.7: "An exothermic process releases heat to the surroundings, so the surroundings become warmer."]
why-not C: Endothermic processes absorb heat; they do not release it. [p.7: "An endothermic process absorbs heat from the surroundings"]
why-not D: Heat is exactly the energy that moves between bodies at different temperatures. [p.6: "Heat (q) is the transfer of thermal energy between two bodies at different temperatures."]
covers: LO-2.1-3, T-endothermic-process, T-exothermic-process
:::

::: question Q-2.1-02
type: cloze
bloom: remember
ask: The ____ are everything outside the system that can exchange energy with it.
answer: surroundings
why: This is how the book defines the surroundings. [p.7: "The surroundings are everything outside the system that can exchange energy with it."]
covers: LO-2.1-2, T-surroundings
:::

::: question Q-2.1-03
type: tf
bloom: understand
ask: A bathtub of warm water and a cup of water at the same temperature always transfer the same amount of heat.
answer: false
why: The amount of heat transferred depends on the amount of matter, but temperature does not. [p.6: "Temperature does not depend on the amount of matter present, whereas the amount of heat transferred does."]
covers: LO-2.1-1, T-heat, T-temperature
:::

::: question Q-2.1-04
type: mcq
bloom: remember
ask: In which direction does heat flow spontaneously?
option A: From a colder body to a hotter body
option B: From a hotter body to a colder body
option C: Only from a liquid to a solid
option D: Always from the surroundings into the system
answer: B
why: Heat flows by itself from a hotter body to a colder body. [p.6: "Heat always flows spontaneously from a hotter body to a colder body until both reach the same temperature."]
why-not A: That is the opposite of the direction the book gives. [p.6: "Heat always flows spontaneously from a hotter body to a colder body"]
why-not C: The rule is about hotter and colder bodies, not about liquids and solids.
why-not D: In an exothermic process heat flows out of the system instead. [p.7: "In an exothermic process, heat flows out of the system."]
covers: LO-2.1-1, T-heat
:::
